opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it comes down to a few things.

First is the data problem. In gaming, you have essentially infinite data. You can spin up thousands of copies of a game, run them faster than real time, and the agent can die a million times and nobody cares. In robotics, every bit of data has to come from the physical world, and the physical world runs at one second per second. You can't parallelize it the way you can a simulator, robots are expensive, they break, and someone has to reset the scene after every trial. So data is the fundamental bottleneck.

Second is the embodiment gap. In a game, the action space is clean: you press a button, and the character does exactly what you told it to. In the real world, you're dealing with motors, friction, contact dynamics, sensor noise, and latency. Picking up a cup sounds trivial, but the contact physics of fingers on a slightly deformable object is incredibly hard to model. Moravec's paradox captures it well: the things that are easy for us, like walking or grasping, are the hardest for machines, while the things we find hard, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy.

Third is the sim-to-real gap. We'd love to just train in simulation like we do for games, and we're making real progress there with GPU-accelerated physics and domain randomization. But simulation is always an approximation. The textures, lighting, and physics are never quite right, so a policy that works perfectly in sim can fall apart the moment you deploy it.

And finally, the stakes are different. In a game, failure is free. In the real world, a robot that fails can break itself, break things around it, or hurt someone. That changes how much exploration you can afford.

So I like to think of gaming as a sandbox where we can develop the algorithms and ideas, like open-ended learning, skill libraries, and foundation models for agents, and robotics as the much harder final exam where those ideas have to survive contact with reality. The good news is that the recipe is starting to converge: combine internet-scale video and language data, massive simulation, and a smaller amount of real robot data, and train one foundation model across all of it. I think that's how we'll eventually crack it.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the sim-to-real gap as a robotics difficulty: policies trained in simulation must be deployed in the real world.

r002.rationale: It explains that simulation is only an approximation, with mismatched textures, lighting, and physics causing a policy that succeeds in simulation to fail after deployment.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts gaming with real-world robotics but does not clearly state that gaming agents are trained and tested in the same environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I actually came to robotics from gaming. My earlier work was on Minecraft, agents like MineDojo and Voyager, and in that world you have this incredible luxury: the simulator is the world. You can run thousands of copies in parallel, step the environment a million times, reset whenever you want, and it costs you basically nothing but GPU time. Reward is often well defined, or at least you can extract it. And the biggest thing is that the data is already there. The internet is full of Minecraft videos, wikis, Reddit threads. Gaming has a huge internet-scale corpus you can bootstrap from.

Robotics breaks almost every one of those assumptions. First, physics is unforgiving. In a game, if the collision model is a bit off, nobody cares. In the real world, a few millimeters of error means the mug slips out of the gripper. So the sim-to-real gap is a real tax you pay on everything.

Second, you can't reset reality. If a robot knocks over a glass, somebody has to go clean it up. Real-world data is slow, expensive, and dangerous to collect, so you're orders of magnitude more data-starved than in gaming. We're talking thousands of hours of teleoperation versus trillions of tokens for language models. That's the data problem, and I think it's the single hardest thing in the field right now.

Third, the action space is continuous and high-dimensional. In Minecraft, the actions are discrete: move, jump, craft. A humanoid has dozens of joints that need to be controlled at hundreds of hertz with contact dynamics. That's a much harder control problem.

And finally, there's no ground truth reward in the real world. Nobody tells the robot "plus one" when it folds a shirt correctly. You have to either engineer that or learn it.

So my view is that the answer is to make robotics look more like gaming. That's why I'm so excited about simulation at scale, about generative models that can act as world simulators, about synthesizing data rather than only collecting it. If we can get the simulator to be good enough and fast enough, we bring back those gaming superpowers: infinite parallel worlds, infinite resets, infinite data. That's the path to a foundation model for embodied agents.

r001.rationale: It identifies the sim-to-real gap as a difficulty in robotics, describing it as a tax on robotics.

r002.rationale: It explains that an inaccurate collision model or millimeter-scale error can make real-world robotic behavior fail, illustrating why transfer from simulation is difficult.

r003.rationale: It says the simulator is the world in gaming, but does not state that gaming agents are both trained and tested in that same environment.

astra-6.text:
The big difference is that in gaming, you control the world. You can run thousands of environments in parallel, reset them instantly, and let an agent fail millions of times. The simulator gives you a clear interface for taking actions and often a clear signal for whether you’re succeeding.

In robotics, you have to earn every bit of that infrastructure. If a robot drops something, someone may have to pick it up. If it falls, it can break. And the real world is full of details that are hard to simulate accurately—friction, contact, deformable objects, even changes in lighting. A policy can work beautifully in simulation and then fail on the physical robot.

So you have two problems at once: learning intelligent behavior and making that behavior survive the gap between your training environment and reality. Simulation helps you get scale, but transferring that learning reliably into the physical world is the hard part.

r001.rationale: It identifies transferring learned behavior from simulation to the physical world as a major added challenge in robotics.

r002.rationale: It says real-world details are hard to simulate accurately and that a policy successful in simulation may fail on the robot.

r003.rationale: It describes gaming environments and their clear interfaces, but does not state that gaming agents are trained and tested in the same environment.

sol-6.1.text:
Gaming gives you a world that’s already a simulator. You can run thousands of copies in parallel, reset whenever you fail, and get a clear signal about whether you’re making progress. A robot has to deal with a physical world that doesn’t offer those conveniences. If it drops something or falls over, someone may have to step in, and collecting another attempt takes real time.

There’s also a much harder interface between perception and action. Knowing what an object is doesn’t mean you know how to grasp it. Small differences in friction, weight, or contact can change the outcome. And even if you train in simulation, the policy has to survive those differences when you put it on real hardware.

So you’re solving both a learning problem and a data problem: how do you generate enough diverse experience, safely and cheaply, for an agent that needs to work beyond the situations it has already seen?

r001.rationale: It says a policy trained in simulation must still work when placed on real hardware, identifying sim-to-real transfer as an added robotics challenge.

r002.rationale: It notes that small physical differences in friction, weight, or contact can change outcomes and that the policy must withstand those differences on real hardware.

r003.rationale: It describes gaming as a simulator with parallel runs and resets, but does not state that gaming agents are trained and tested in the same environment.
